title: Lamrim: precious human life
hookLine: the freedoms and chances of this life, rare and precious

lines: A YOKE ADRIFT ON THE OCEAN.
cards: The Buddha asks his monks to picture something odd. A wooden yoke, the kind laid across an ox's neck, with a single hole in it, tossed into a great ocean. Wind blows it east, then west.
Somewhere under the water lives a blind turtle that comes up for air only rarely. How likely is it that the turtle, rising, pushes its head right through the hole in that drifting yoke? Not very.
Lamrim teachers begin their staircase right here: with how unlikely, and how valuable, this ordinary life is.

teach.h: THE BLIND TURTLE AND THE YOKE.
teach.b: You met the blind turtle on day three hundred forty-seven; here it becomes the first stair. First, the turtle.
In the Pali texts, the Buddha asks his monks whether the blind turtle would ever put its neck through the yoke's hole. They say it might, someday, after a very long time.
He answers that it would happen sooner than a being in the lower realms reaching a human birth again. This life, the ordinary weekday one, is a long shot that came in. Second, what makes it precious.
Lamrim teachers don't say a life is precious only because it's human.
They point to particular freedoms and chances. Freedom from conditions where practice is impossible: constant pain, constant fear, no time to think.
And chances: a mind that can learn, a teaching within reach, people who can explain it, a little room to try. In Tibetan this pair is called dal jor, freedoms and endowments. Third, the Dhammapada.

teach.h: HARD TO GET HERE, HARD TO HEAR IT.
teach.b: Among the hard things it lists: being born human is hard, and hearing the true teaching is hard. If both have happened, something rare has lined up.
Fourth, why the staircase starts here. It isn't meant to make anyone feel lucky and move on. It's meant to make the rest of the path feel worth climbing.
If this life is a lottery ticket that already won, wasting the afternoon isn't a small thing, and using even ten quiet minutes of it isn't small either.

how: In lamrim teaching, students begin by meditating on the freedoms and endowments of a precious human life, reflecting on how rare and useful it is before moving to the next stage.

o: the first stair: a life spent apart from the world
the first stair: tackling the highest teaching first
the first stair: this rare human life and its freedoms

games.q: precious human life: tap the pairs.
p: not trapped in constant pain or fear

s: in the story, the turtle reaching the yoke is easier than a human birth
the Buddha says the turtle would manage it sooner than a being in the lower realms reaching human birth.
lamrim calls life precious only because it is human
it points to particular freedoms and chances, like time, a mind that can learn and a teaching in reach.
this stage is meant to make you feel lucky and move on

games.q: you've realized this life is a long shot that came in. it's a free afternoon. what does the lamrim suggest?
o: relax: it's already won, so nothing matters.
use even a little of it well, because it's rare.
worry about wasting it until the afternoon is gone.
games.why: the point of the first stair is that the path is worth climbing: even ten quiet minutes of this life aren't small.

practice: Slowly name three freedoms you have right now: maybe a quiet minute, a mind that can follow a teaching, someone, somewhere, who taught you something true. Don't hurry past them.
After the third, let them sit together, and simply notice that they're here at the same time.

wordCard.voice: Lamrim, the first stair: precious human life. The freedoms and chances of this life, rare as a blind turtle finding the yoke. Today's word.

orig.note: Tibetan: dal 'byor, the freedoms and endowments of a precious human life.

carryVoice: Your line: this precious life. A long shot that came in. Back tomorrow, same hill.
